name: Graham
who: Retired electrician. Lives with his wife. Brother had a heart attack at 70.

actions.label: Side effects?
actions.text: No problems with the tablets. Takes them every morning.

actions.label: Smoking
actions.text: Ex-smoker. Quit 10 years ago after 30 years.

actions.label: Ideas, concerns, expectations
actions.text: Thinks his blood pressure is "sorted". Quietly worried about his brother's heart attack. Expects a script and the car park.

actions.label: "Anything else?"
actions.doorknob: "Oh, and by the way, I get a bit tight in the chest walking up the hill to the shops. Goes away when I stop."
actions.why: "Anything else?" was where the angina was hiding.

actions.label: Chest tightness: tell me more
actions.text: Central tightness on exertion for about 6 weeks. Eases within a few minutes of resting. Never at rest. None today.
actions.why: Characterising exertional chest pain is the whole consult once it's mentioned.

actions.label: Blood pressure
actions.text: 142/86. Pulse 78, regular.

actions.label: Heart, lungs, ankles
actions.text: Normal heart sounds, clear chest, no ankle swelling.

actions.label: ECG
actions.text: Sinus rhythm, no acute changes. A normal resting ECG doesn't rule out angina.
actions.why: New exertional chest pain earns an ECG today.

actions.label: Order lipids, HbA1c, kidney check
actions.text: Ordered: lipids, HbA1c, eGFR and urine albumin-creatinine ratio.

options: Stable blood pressure. Script only.
Probable stable angina
Chest wall (musculoskeletal) pain
Acute coronary syndrome: call 000 now
Renew his blood pressure medicine
Short-acting GTN spray, with clear instructions
Prompt cardiology assessment for further testing
Lipids, HbA1c and kidney check, and a CVD risk review
Explain the plan and check he's understood (teach-back)
Reassure: probably just unfit. See you in 12 months
Start antibiotics
Call 000 if chest pain comes on at rest, is severe, is getting worse, or isn't fully gone within 10 minutes
Mention it at your next review if it's still there
Take two paracetamol and lie down
Drive yourself to ED if it gets bad

pearl: The "just a script" consult is where angina likes to hide. Leave room for "anything else?", and if the answer is chest pain on exertion, the plan isn't "see you next year".

name: Graham
criticalWhy: Chest pain at rest in the waiting room. Every minute in the queue is heart muscle.
who: Back again. You saw him for a repeat script.
opening: "It's happening walking to the letterbox now. Had a bad one this morning just sitting down."

actions.label: How has the pain changed?
actions.text: Now with minimal effort, and twice at rest. This morning's lasted about 15 minutes.
actions.why: Pain at rest or on minimal effort is the change that makes this unstable.

actions.label: Any pain right now?
actions.text: Mild tightness now. Started about 20 minutes ago in the waiting room.
actions.why: Ongoing pain right now changes everything about the next ten minutes.

actions.label: Ideas, concerns, expectations
actions.text: Scared it's a heart attack, like his brother. Hoping for "a stronger pill".

actions.label: "Anything else?"
actions.text: "Isn't that enough?" Fair.

actions.label: Obs: BP, pulse, sats
actions.text: BP 150/90, HR 92, sats 96% on air. Pale and clammy.
actions.why: Obs tell you how sick he is right now and whether GTN is safe.

actions.label: 12-lead ECG
actions.text: ST depression in the lateral leads.
actions.why: The ECG is quick and changes the urgency, but it shouldn't delay calling the ambulance.

actions.label: Send a troponin to the lab
actions.text: Result in hours. He needs a hospital, not a courier.
actions.why: A community troponin delays transfer and doesn't change what he needs.

options: Unstable angina / acute coronary syndrome
Stable angina
Reflux
Anxiety
Call 000 for urgent ambulance transfer
Aspirin 300 mg, chewed or dissolved (unless contraindicated)
GTN spray while waiting, watching his blood pressure
Routine oxygen even though his sats are 96%
Explain what's happening and why
Send him home with a stronger tablet
Book an outpatient stress test next month
Stay with him, keep him monitored and send a summary with the ambulance
Let him wait in the car park for the ambulance
He can drive himself to hospital
Come back if it happens again

pearl: Angina that's new, worse or happening at rest is an acute coronary syndrome until proven otherwise. Aspirin, ECG, ambulance, in whichever order gets them all done fastest.

name: Maya
criticalWhy: A floppy, feverish toddler is time-critical. Seeing her last means she waited longest.
who: Here with her dad, Emeka. Usually a chatterbox.
opening: "She's been hot since last night. Now she just wants to lie on me."

actions.label: Fever story
actions.text: Fever since last night. Vomited twice. Refusing drinks; only one wet nappy today.

actions.label: Immunisations
actions.text: Up to date for her age.

actions.label: Ideas, concerns, expectations
actions.text: "She's never been like this." He wants her checked properly, and he's right to.

actions.label: "Anything else?"
actions.doorknob: "She screamed when I touched her legs this morning. She never does that."
actions.why: Leg pain is an early warning sign of meningococcal sepsis in children.

actions.label: Obs: temp, heart rate, cap refill
actions.text: Temp 39.4°C, HR 170, capillary refill 4 seconds. Cold hands and feet.
actions.why: Cold peripheries and slow cap refill in a febrile child are early sepsis signs.

actions.label: Check her skin all over
actions.text: Several purple spots on her legs that don't fade when you press a glass on them.
actions.why: A non-blanching rash with fever is meningococcal disease until proven otherwise.

actions.label: Neck and alertness
actions.text: Drowsy and irritable when handled. Neck hard to assess.

actions.label: Urine dipstick
actions.text: Three minutes of coaxing, no sample. The clock didn't wait.
actions.why: A urine sample was never going to change the plan for this child.

options: Viral illness
Suspected meningococcal sepsis
Urinary tract infection
Gastroenteritis
Call 000 for urgent transfer
Parenteral antibiotics (benzylpenicillin or ceftriaxone) now, as long as it doesn't delay transfer
Phone the receiving hospital and hand over
Explain to her dad what's happening and why
Paracetamol, fluids and review tomorrow
Oral antibiotics and home
Stay with them until the ambulance arrives
Back to the waiting room until the ambulance comes
Dad can drive her to ED if traffic's OK
Come back tomorrow if she's no better

pearl: In a febrile child: leg pain, cold hands and feet and pale or mottled skin can come before the rash. Once there's a non-blanching rash, antibiotics and an ambulance shouldn't wait for anything.

name: Priya
who: Accountant. Two kids under five. Vegetarian.
opening: "I'm just exhausted. I figured it's work."

actions.label: Mood and sleep
actions.text: Mood fine, still enjoys things. Sleeps 7 hours. No snoring.

actions.label: Diet
actions.text: Vegetarian, eats a varied diet.

actions.label: Ideas, concerns, expectations
actions.text: Wonders about her thyroid (her mum has hypothyroidism). Expects blood tests.

actions.label: "Anything else?"
actions.doorknob: "Also... my periods have got really heavy. I'm flooding through pads overnight."
actions.why: Heavy periods were the cause, and she only mentioned them because you asked.

actions.label: Periods: tell me more
actions.text: Heavy for 7 days with clots, changing pads every 1 to 2 hours on heavy days. Regular cycle. No bleeding between periods or after sex.
actions.why: A bleeding history shapes both the diagnosis and whether she needs imaging.

actions.label: Obs and colour
actions.text: Pale. HR 96, BP 112/70.

actions.label: Pelvic examination (with consent)
actions.text: With consent: no masses, uterus feels normal size.

actions.label: Full blood count and ferritin
actions.text: Hb 98 g/L (low). Ferritin 6 µg/L (typical range for women roughly 30 to 300).
actions.why: The standard says to check FBC and ferritin routinely in heavy menstrual bleeding.

actions.label: Thyroid function
actions.text: TSH normal.

actions.label: Pregnancy test
actions.text: Negative.

options: Burnout
Iron deficiency anaemia from heavy menstrual bleeding
Hypothyroidism
Depression
Start iron replacement
Discuss treatment for the heavy bleeding (e.g. hormonal IUD, tranexamic acid, NSAIDs)
Explain the plan and check she's understood (teach-back)
Pelvic ultrasound for everyone with heavy periods, regardless
Refer for gastroscopy and colonoscopy
More red meat and an early night
Come back sooner if you're breathless, faint, have chest pain, or the bleeding gets heavier
Nothing to worry about
See you in a year
Stop the iron if your stools go dark

pearl: "Tired all the time" in a menstruating woman: ask about periods, then check FBC and ferritin. The hormonal IUD is the most effective medical treatment for heavy bleeding when there's no significant pathology.

sources.t: Heavy Menstrual Bleeding Clinical Care Standard
Lifeblood: causes of iron deficiency anaemia

name: Tom
who: Apprentice carpenter. Started deadlifting last month.
opening: "Did deadlifts Saturday and my back's killing me. Can I get a scan and something strong?"

actions.label: Pain story
actions.text: Low back ache, worse bending. No pain down the legs.

actions.label: Bladder, bowel, saddle numbness
actions.text: No trouble passing urine, no bowel change, no numbness "down below".
actions.why: Cauda equina symptoms are the one thing you can't afford to skip in back pain.

actions.label: Fever, weight loss, cancer, injecting
actions.text: None.
actions.why: Screening for infection, malignancy and fracture is part of every back pain assessment.

actions.label: Ideas, concerns, expectations
actions.text: Thinks he's "slipped a disc". Worried he'll lose his apprenticeship. Expects an MRI and oxycodone.

actions.label: "Anything else?"
actions.text: "Nah, that's it."

actions.label: Leg neuro exam
actions.text: Normal power, reflexes and sensation.
actions.why: A focused neuro exam is how you show yourself there's no nerve compromise.

actions.label: Back exam
actions.text: Tender muscles either side of the spine. Bending forward limited by pain.

actions.label: Lumbar X-ray
actions.text: Normal. Which you could have predicted.
actions.why: Imaging wasn't indicated: no red flags.

actions.label: MRI request
actions.text: Without alerting features, imaging isn't recommended, and incidental disc findings can frighten people.
actions.why: An MRI without red flags tends to find things that aren't the problem.

options: Non-specific low back pain
Cauda equina syndrome
Disc prolapse needing surgery
Spinal fracture
Stay active and keep doing usual activities, modified as needed
Simple pain relief to help him keep moving
Explain the plan and why no scan is needed (teach-back)
Review in 1 to 2 weeks if not improving
Oxycodone for two weeks
A week of bed rest
Order an MRI
Come back the same day if you get bladder or bowel problems, numbness around the genitals or bottom, or leg weakness
Come back if it's not gone in 6 months
No need to come back
Take more tablets if it hurts more

pearl: Most acute back pain settles. Screen for red flags, examine, then sell activity. Bed rest is harmful and opioids are for carefully selected patients, lowest dose, shortest time.

sources.t: Low Back Pain Clinical Care Standard

name: June
criticalWhy: A head injury on an anticoagulant can bleed quietly. Seeing her last cost her hours.
who: Lives alone, gardens daily. Her daughter Eleni brought her in.
blurb: Fell last night. Daughter "a bit worried".
opening: "I'm fine, love. Eleni made me come."

actions.label: What happened?
actions.text: Tripped on a rug getting up to the toilet. Hit her head on the bedside table.
actions.why: A head strike changes this from a fall to a head injury.

actions.label: Medicines
actions.text: Apixaban for atrial fibrillation. Blood pressure tablet.
actions.why: Anticoagulation is the detail that makes this head injury urgent.

actions.label: Headache, vomiting, drowsiness
actions.text: Headache since. Vomited once this morning.
actions.why: Headache and vomiting after a head injury need asking about every time.

actions.label: Ideas, concerns, expectations
actions.text: Worried she'll be "put in a home". Wants a quick check and to get back to her tomatoes.

actions.label: "Anything else?" (to Eleni too)
actions.doorknob: Eleni: "She's been asking me the same question over and over this morning."
actions.why: New repetitive questioning after a head injury is a worrying change.

actions.label: Obs
actions.text: BP 150/80, HR 88 irregular. Alert, but asks you the same thing twice.

actions.label: Head and neuro exam
actions.text: Bruise over the right temple. No focal weakness.

actions.label: Finger-prick glucose
actions.text: 6.1 mmol/L.

actions.label: Routine bloods
actions.text: Results tomorrow. Not much use today.
actions.why: Routine bloods don't answer the question that matters today: is she bleeding inside her head?

options: Simple mechanical fall, no injury
Head injury while on an anticoagulant: needs urgent CT
Stroke
Urinary tract infection causing confusion
Same-day transfer to ED for a CT head scan
Explain the plan to June and Eleni, and check they've understood
Restart and carry on with apixaban as usual
Ice pack and home with Eleni
If she gets drowsier, more confused, vomits again or the headache worsens before she's seen, call 000
Watch her overnight at home
Come back next week
Let her sleep it off

pearl: NICE suggests considering a CT head within 8 hours of injury for anyone on an anticoagulant, even with no other indication. Add vomiting and new repetitive questioning, and the decision makes itself.

name: Jayden
who: Aboriginal boy from a remote community. Here with his nan, Aunty Rose.
opening: Aunty Rose: "He's had a sore throat for two days and he's off his food."

actions.label: Symptoms
actions.text: Sore throat and fever. No cough.

actions.label: Rheumatic fever history
actions.text: His cousin has rheumatic heart disease. Jayden hasn't had rheumatic fever.
actions.why: Living in a high-risk setting, with family history, is what decides treatment.

actions.label: Skin sores
actions.text: A few healing school sores on his legs.

actions.label: Ideas, concerns, expectations
actions.text: Aunty Rose asks if he'll need "the needle every month" like his cousin. Hopes he's back at school soon.

actions.label: "Anything else?"
actions.text: "No, that's it."

actions.label: Throat and neck
actions.text: Red tonsils, tender neck glands.

actions.label: Heart and joints
actions.text: No murmur. No joint swelling.

actions.label: Throat swab
actions.text: Sent. In a high-risk setting, treatment shouldn't wait for it.

options: Viral sore throat: no treatment needed
Sore throat in a child at high risk of acute rheumatic fever
Acute rheumatic fever
Peritonsillar abscess (quinsy)
Penicillin treatment now (first-line for sore throat in high-risk groups)
Treat the skin sores as well
Explain to Jayden and Aunty Rose, and answer the needle question honestly
Symptom relief only
Wait for the swab before deciding
Come back if he gets sore or swollen joints, breathlessness or chest pain, or isn't improving in a few days
Only come back if the throat's still sore in a month
No need to come back
Come back if he gets a cough

pearl: Where rheumatic fever is common, a sore throat or skin sore is a prevention opportunity. Treat with penicillin, treat the skin, and make sure follow-up is easy.

name: Mei
who: Primary school teacher. Last period 2 years ago.
opening: "The night sweats are wrecking my sleep. My friend says HRT changed her life."

actions.label: Symptoms
actions.text: About 10 flushes a day. Wakes drenched most nights.

actions.label: Past history
actions.text: No personal history of breast cancer or blood clots. Non-smoker.

actions.label: Ideas, concerns, expectations
actions.text: Worried hormones cause cancer. Hoping to leave with a script today.

actions.label: "Anything else?"
actions.doorknob: "Oh, I've had a bit of spotting the last couple of months. Probably nothing?"
actions.why: Bleeding after menopause needs investigating before MHT starts.

actions.label: Spotting: tell me more
actions.text: Light spotting three times in two months. No pain.
actions.why: Postmenopausal bleeding is a red flag in its own right.

actions.label: Speculum exam (with consent)
actions.text: Cervix looks normal. No obvious source of bleeding.

options: Menopause symptoms: straightforward MHT
Menopause symptoms plus postmenopausal bleeding that needs investigating
Thyroid disease
Periods coming back: normal
Investigate the bleeding first (transvaginal ultrasound, then gynaecology as needed)
When MHT is appropriate: combined oestrogen and progestogen, as she has a uterus
Explain the plan and check she's understood (teach-back)
Start oestrogen-only MHT today
Tell her spotting is normal after menopause
Let us know about any further bleeding, and come back for the ultrasound results
Ignore the spotting
Come back in a year
Stop worrying about it

pearl: MHT is the most effective treatment for hot flushes, but any unexplained vaginal bleeding gets investigated before it's prescribed. With a uterus, oestrogen always comes with a progestogen.

name: Sam
who: Works in hospitality. Uses they/them. Plays club rugby.
opening: "I just need something to help me sleep."

actions.label: Sleep
actions.text: Awake until 3am most nights for two months.

actions.label: Mood and interest
actions.text: Low most days. Stopped going to training. Eating less.

actions.label: Ask directly about suicide
actions.text: "Sometimes I think everyone'd be better off without me." No plan. No previous attempts.
actions.why: Asking directly is safe, and people often won't volunteer it unless asked.

actions.label: Alcohol and drugs
actions.text: Drinking more on weekends.

actions.label: Ideas, concerns, expectations
actions.text: Thinks it's "just stress". Worried about being judged. Hoped for sleeping tablets.

actions.label: "Anything else?"
actions.doorknob: "My housemate moved out last month. It's pretty quiet at home now."

actions.label: Mental state
actions.text: Flat, quiet, good eye contact. No signs of injury.

actions.label: Depression questionnaire
actions.text: Scores in the severe range.

options: Insomnia only
Depression with suicidal thoughts
Bipolar disorder
Alcohol use disorder
Make a safety plan together (warning signs, people and services to contact)
Arrange psychological therapy
Book a review within days, not months
Crisis contacts: Lifeline 13 11 14, or 000 in an emergency
Explain the plan and check they've understood
Sleeping tablets and a review in 3 months
If the thoughts get stronger or you start making plans: call 000 or Lifeline (13 11 14), or go to ED
Come back if you're still not sleeping in 3 months
Try not to think about it
Have a drink to help you sleep

pearl: "Can't sleep" is a common ticket of entry for depression. Ask about suicide directly and kindly; it doesn't plant the idea, and it may be the only way you find out.

name: Sam
criticalWhy: Someone at immediate risk sat in the waiting room the longest.
who: Back again, with their friend Jess. You saw Sam about sleep.
opening: Jess: "Sam sent me a message last night that really scared me."

actions.label: Ask directly about suicide
actions.text: "I've been thinking about it a lot. I looked up ways last night."
actions.why: You can't judge risk without asking directly.

actions.label: Access to means
actions.text: Has been saving up tablets at home.
actions.why: Access to means is one of the most modifiable risks.

actions.label: Who's around?
actions.text: Jess can stay with Sam today.

actions.label: Ideas, concerns, expectations
actions.text: Sam is ashamed and frightened. Jess wants to know Sam will be safe tonight.

actions.label: "Anything else?"
actions.text: "I didn't tell you everything last time."

actions.label: Mental state
actions.text: Tearful, hopeless. Says they can't keep themselves safe right now.
actions.why: Whether they can stay safe right now decides where they go next.

actions.label: Routine bloods
actions.text: Not the priority right now.
actions.why: Bloods can wait. Safety can't.

options: Depression with high, immediate suicide risk
Adjustment reaction, low risk
Insomnia
Urgent same-day crisis assessment (acute mental health team or ED)
Sam isn't left alone: Jess stays until handover
Reduce access to means (the saved tablets)
Explain what happens next, to Sam and Jess
Home with a review in a fortnight
If at any point Sam can't stay safe before the assessment: call 000
See how tonight goes
Book a fortnightly review
Leave it to Sam to decide

pearl: When someone can't keep themselves safe, the plan is same-day crisis care, someone with them, and less access to means. Ask, act, and hand over warmly.

name: Abdi
who: Arrived in Australia 4 months ago as a refugee. Somali speaker. Just started work as a delivery driver.
opening: (In Somali, gesturing to a form) "Cough... and the form, for my job."

actions.label: Book a phone interpreter (TIS)
actions.text: A Somali interpreter joins. Now you can actually take a history.

actions.label: Cough details
actions.text: Cough for 6 weeks. Some blood-streaked sputum.
actions.why: A cough over three weeks, especially with blood, is a TB flag.

actions.label: Fevers, sweats, weight
actions.text: Night sweats. Lost about 6 kg.
actions.why: Night sweats and weight loss complete the TB picture.

actions.label: Who lives with you?
actions.text: His wife and three children.

actions.label: Ideas, concerns, expectations
actions.text: Worried he'll lose his new job. Expects cough medicine and a signed form.

actions.label: "Anything else?"
actions.doorknob: "My cousin had TB in the camp."
actions.why: A known TB contact raises the stakes considerably.

actions.label: Chest and temperature
actions.text: Crackles at the right upper chest. Temp 37.8°C.

actions.label: Chest X-ray and sputum for TB
actions.text: Requested: chest X-ray and sputum samples for TB testing.
actions.why: Chest X-ray and sputum are the first tests for suspected lung TB.

options: Viral bronchitis
Suspected pulmonary tuberculosis
Asthma
Reflux cough
Chest X-ray and sputum tests for TB
Contact the local TB (chest) clinic urgently: assessment and treatment are free
Explain the plan through the interpreter and check understanding
Cough syrup and sign the fit-for-work form
Come back urgently if you cough more blood or get breathless
Come back if the cough lasts another 6 weeks
No need to come back
Just keep working

pearl: A cough of 3 weeks or more with sweats and weight loss in someone from a high-TB setting needs a chest X-ray and sputum. And a professional interpreter, not a mime.

name: Lachlan
who: Has Down syndrome. Lives in supported accommodation, works at a café. Here with his support worker, Kelly.
opening: Lachlan: "I'm tired. I want to go to work."

actions.label: Ask Lachlan himself
actions.text: Lachlan tells you he's "cold all the time" and his "tummy is stuck" (constipated).

actions.label: History from Kelly (with his OK)
actions.text: Slower at work over 6 months, gained 5 kg, dry skin. No change in routine or living situation.

actions.label: When was his thyroid last checked?
actions.text: No record of a TSH test in 3 years.
actions.why: People with Down syndrome have a much higher risk of hypothyroidism, rising with age.

actions.label: Ideas, concerns, expectations
actions.text: Lachlan wants to keep his café job. Kelly is worried it's "early dementia".

actions.label: "Anything else?"
actions.text: Kelly: "He's been falling asleep on the bus home."

actions.label: Obs and examination
actions.text: HR 56. Weight up 5 kg. Dry skin. Slow-relaxing reflexes.

actions.label: TSH and free T4
actions.text: TSH 38 mIU/L (typical range about 0.4 to 4), free T4 low.
actions.why: A thyroid test is the cheapest test that rules a treatable cause in or out.

options: Early dementia
Hypothyroidism
Depression
"Just part of Down syndrome"
Start thyroid hormone replacement with a follow-up TSH
Explain to Lachlan in plain language, check he's understood, and include Kelly with his OK
Regular thyroid checks from now on
Refer to a memory clinic for dementia
Repeat the blood test in about 6 weeks, and come back sooner if he's getting worse
Nothing to follow up
Come back next year
Only come back if he stops working

pearl: Don't let a disability explain away new symptoms (diagnostic overshadowing). Talk to the patient first, then the support worker, and check the thyroid.

sources.t: NICE indicator IND79: TSH testing in Down syndrome
Pathology Tests Explained: free T4 and TSH
